title: A city on soft ground
subtitle: Seattle and Bellevue, Washington

technical.title: Slow ground settling, Seattle and Bellevue (layout, placeholder data)
technical.subtitle: Synthetic millimeter-scale settling in filled ground, NISAR-style L-band geometry
technical.summary: Placeholder line-of-sight displacement for slow settling in soft, filled ground (Duwamish/SODO, Kent valley) over about a year. Real urban motion here is millimeters per year, so a real map would be built from a stack of many 12-day passes with a fitted velocity, not one pair. Replace the grids once a coverage check shows a usable NISAR time series.
caveats: All displacement and coherence values are synthetic placeholders.
Real motion in the urban area is only millimeters per year. One interferogram will not show it; a time series is needed.
Water bodies are masked roughly in the placeholder. A real map uses the product's own mask.
A single line of sight cannot separate vertical from horizontal motion.

storyText: Seattle and Bellevue sit on a basin of soft sediment, and parts of the waterfront are built on fill. Soft ground can settle slowly, and it can shake harder in an earthquake. Radar from space can measure millimeters of settling across the whole city.
credits: Imagery © Esri · Terrain: AWS Terrain Tiles · Layout preview with placeholder data

why.title: Why would a city sink?
why.body: Ground made of soft clay, silt or human-placed fill compacts over time, and pumping groundwater can speed it up. The waterfront south of downtown and the Kent valley are on this kind of ground. The motion is slow, often just millimeters a year.

why.title: Why does soft ground matter in an earthquake?
why.body: Soft sediment in a basin can amplify and prolong shaking, and water-saturated fill can lose its strength (liquefaction). Seattle also sits near the Seattle Fault, which has ruptured in the past. Knowing which ground is soft helps decide where to look closely.

why.title: How can radar see millimeters?
why.body: NISAR measures the distance to the ground using the phase of its L-band radar echo. A shift of a few millimeters per year is tiny, so scientists stack many passes taken every 12 days and fit a trend. That is why this story needs a year of data, not one pair.

why.title: What can the map not tell us?
why.body: It shows motion along the satellite's slanted line of sight, relative to a reference point, not the cause. Radar also loses signal over water and dense forest, which is why the lakes and the Sound are blank.

tour.title: Seattle and Bellevue
tour.text: Two cities on either side of Lake Washington, built on a sediment-filled basin between the Cascades and Puget Sound.

tour.title: NISAR looks once
tour.text: NISAR images the area and records exact distances to the ground. This is the 'before' picture. (Placeholder date.)

tour.title: A year of passes
tour.text: NISAR returns every 12 days. Stacking a year of passes lets scientists pull out very slow motion. (Placeholder dates.)

tour.title: The waterfront settles
tour.text: Orange areas moved away from the satellite, which here mostly means the ground sank slightly. The soft, filled ground south of downtown shows the most. (Placeholder pattern.)

tour.title: Across the lake
tour.text: Bellevue sits on firmer ground, so its pattern is much smaller. (Placeholder pattern.)

tour.title: How sure are we?
tour.text: Water and thick forest scramble the radar, so those areas are blank. We hide what we cannot trust.
